note: Single source of truth for the named TreeUI practices. Consumed by the landing page (apps/landing), the Storybook Foundation/Practices page and per-story practice notes (apps/docs), and the AI catalog (packages/mcp). If a component starts or stops following a practice, update this file in the same change.

philosophy.statement: TreeUI is optimized for clarity — visual clarity for users and development clarity for teams — with consistency and accessibility as defaults, never opt-ins. Components are tuned for good UI and UX through the named practices below, and the library takes on layout and alignment work so product code doesn't have to.
pillars: Clarity over decoration — in the interface and in the API.
Consistency and accessibility are defaults, not options.
Good UI and UX through named, well-defined practices.
The library absorbs layout and alignment busywork.

practices.title: Visual interaction feedback
practices.summary: Every interaction answers back. Hover, focus, active, loading, and disabled are designed states — never afterthoughts left to the consumer.
rules: Interactive surfaces ship hover, press (:active), and focus-visible treatments out of the box — each a colour change, never motion alone.
Hover, press, selected and disabled colours are derived by the token layer from the semantic palette, so a product that supplies one accent gets a complete, contrast-checked state set.
Every state is measurably distinguishable from the state it replaces; the token validator fails a build where it is not.
Loading states announce themselves (aria-busy plus a labelled, localizable spinner), replace the resting glyph instead of stacking beside it, and block duplicate activation.
Disabled is a colour held at the 3:1 UI floor, not an opacity — opacity cannot be measured for contrast.
Disabled and loading elements never emit activation events.
Focus indicators stay visible in both light and dark themes.

practices.title: Accessible by default
practices.summary: Native semantics first, ARIA where the pattern requires it, full keyboard support, and focus management the consumer never has to write.
rules: Native elements before roles; role="dialog", aria-modal, aria-labelledby only where semantics require them, and no composite-widget role (grid, tree) is claimed without its full keyboard model.
Tab/Shift+Tab order, Escape to close, Enter/Space to activate, arrow keys where the pattern expects them.
Overlays trap focus while open and restore it on close.
Clickable targets stay at or above 44×44px.
Form control boundaries clear 3:1 against every surface (WCAG 1.4.11); decorative edges are a separate token and are not held to it.
A panel anchored to a trigger is rendered in a layer no ancestor can clip, and is pushed back inside the viewport — a control that is painted off-screen or behind a clip is not operable.
Every string a screen reader announces is a prop with a default, never a hard-coded literal; a control whose only name is English is unusable in any other language.

practices.title: One predictable API
practices.summary: The same contracts everywhere: one size scale, one action-variant scale, v-model for form controls, open/close for overlays. Learn one component and you know them all.
rules: Sizes are sm | md | lg across the library.
Action variants come from one scale: solid, outline, ghost, soft, danger.
Form controls speak modelValue + update:modelValue (v-model).
Overlays speak open/defaultOpen + update:open/open-change.

practices.title: Empty, loading, and error are designed states
practices.summary: Screens communicate status honestly: skeletons while loading, purposeful empty states, and status surfaces on one semantic tone scale.
rules: Default, hover, active, focus, disabled, loading, and error/empty states are designed and documented — not just the happy path.
Status tones map to semantic tokens (success, warning, error, info) and pass both themes.
Async feedback is immediate: skeleton or spinner first, toast or alert on completion.

practices.title: Alignment without custom CSS
practices.summary: Layout primitives absorb spacing, alignment, and rhythm so product code never hand-rolls the same flexbox again.
rules: Spacing comes from the --tree-space-* scale, applied by layout components.
Compose TPage, TStack, TGrid, and TSplit before writing a custom layout div.
Forms align through TFormField + TStack + TGrid — labels, hints, and errors line up by contract.
Reading widths and page gutters come from TContainer/TPage, not local max-widths.

A surface takes its container's width: it never grows to the min-content of something inside it. Card, modal and timeline surfaces declare an explicit minmax(0, 1fr) track, and text that can lack a break opportunity wraps, so scrolling and truncation belong to the descendant that asked for them — never to every sibling on the surface.

practices.title: Token-driven clarity
practices.summary: Zero raw colors, spacing, or type in component code. Every visual decision references a --tree-* token, so light/dark and brand theming stay coherent by construction.
rules: Zero hardcoded colours, spacing, or typography in component code — enforced by contract.test.ts, which fails on any literal outside the primitives file.
Colour is three layers: primitives (never referenced), semantics (the public API a product fills in), and derived states (computed by the library, never overridden).
Light and dark are first-class themes; every text/background pair the library renders is measured against WCAG AA in both.
A product themes by seeding one accent; hover, press, tints, the ink on every fill, and both modes are derived from it.
Themes switch by attribute (data-tree-theme) with no component changes.
The documented exceptions are geometry, not design values: focus-ring and hairline widths, sub-pixel motion offsets, and the 44px WCAG target constant.

practices.title: Icons drawn to a contract
practices.summary: Branchline is the drawing contract behind every shipped icon: one grid, one weight, one closed modifier vocabulary. It is checked rather than reviewed — the build renders each glyph and fails when two names look alike at 16px or when a shape draws nothing.
rules: One grid: a 24x24 canvas with geometry inside a 1.5-22.5 trim area, so a 2u stroke never clips; four keylines carry the set — square 17.5, circle 18.5 diameter, wide 18x14, tall 14x18 — and positions land on a 0.25u step.
One weight: 2u stroke, round caps and joins, currentColor and fill=none, all declared on the root <svg>. A child that sets stroke or fill breaks absoluteStrokeWidth and fails the build.
Legible at the size it ships at: every pair of canonical icons is rendered at 16px and must differ by at least 5% of its ink. The rule is measured by branchline.test.ts, not judged by eye.

A modifier gets territory of its own, and the base keeps its size: it is drawn inside bases that enclose space (shield, file, folder, calendar, ticket, message, square, badge, search) and in a cleared corner otherwise, where the base is redrawn at full size with that corner interrupted so 5.5u of canvas stays clear around the mark.
Every shape earns its place: each node is removed and re-rendered, and a node that changes less than 1% of the glyph's ink fails the build. Geometry is never derived from the icon's name.
A family shares one base, drawn once and reused literally; a variant changes exactly one thing, in one place, by one rule.
The metaphor is the conventional one — an icon is not the place to be original. A concept with no settled picture composes one from Branchline primitives, drawn deliberately rather than generated.
One concept, one canonical name, one drawing. A synonym is an alias that shares its target's geometry byte for byte, so mic and microphone can never drift apart.
